The '''13th Academy Awards''' were held on February 27, 1941, to honor films released in [[1940 in film|1940]]. This was the first year that sealed envelopes were used to keep the names of the winners secret.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://oscar.go.com/news/oscar-history/1941-13th-academy-award-winners|title=1941: THE 13TH ACADEMY AWARD WINNERS|date=2014-12-10|publisher=Oscars.org|access-date=2020-02-14}}</ref> The accounting firm of [[Price Waterhouse]] was hired to count the ballots, after voting results in [[12th Academy Awards|1939]] were leaked by the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]''.<ref name="Oscars '40 Notes">{{cite book |last1=Wallechinsky |first1=David |last2=Wallace |first2=Irving |date=1975 |title=The People's Almanac |url=https://archive.org/details/peoplesalmanac00wall/page/834/mode/2up |location=Garden City, New York |publisher=Doubleday & Company, Inc. |page=835 |isbn=0-385-04060-1}}</ref> The gathering was addressed over the radio by President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]].<ref name="Oscars '40 Notes"/>

[[Walter Brennan]]'s victory for his performance in ''[[The Westerner (1940 film)|The Westerner]]'' made him the first actor to win an Academy Award more than twice.<ref name="Oscars '40 Notes"/>

[[Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay|Best Original Screenplay]] was introduced at this ceremony, alongside [[Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay|Best Screenplay]], which would eventually become Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Original Story.

Independent producer [[David O. Selznick]], who had produced the previous year's Best Picture winner ''[[Gone with the Wind (film)|Gone with the Wind]]'' (1939), produced the film with the most nominations again this year, ''[[Rebecca (1940 film)|Rebecca]]'' (11), and campaigned heavily for its win.<ref>''Inside Oscar'', Mason Wiley and Damien Boa, Ballantine Books (1986) pg. 103-107</ref> The film won Best Picture, making Selznick the first to produce two consecutive winners; its only other win was for Best Cinematography (Black and White), marking the last time to date a film would win Best Picture but not win for either directing, acting, or writing.

The film's distributor, [[United Artists]], was the last of the original film studios (Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Columbia, 20th Century-Fox, Warner Bros., RKO Radio, Universal, and Paramount) to win Best Picture. ''Rebecca'' was the first American film directed by [[Alfred Hitchcock]], and the only one of his films to win [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]]. Hitchcock had two films nominated for Best Picture, the other being ''[[Foreign Correspondent (film)|Foreign Correspondent]]'', and two other directors also had two films in the running: Sam Wood (''[[Our Town (1940 film)|Our Town]]'' and ''[[Kitty Foyle (film)|Kitty Foyle]]'') and John Ford (''[[The Long Voyage Home]]'' and ''[[The Grapes of Wrath (film)|The Grapes of Wrath]]'', which won Best Director).

''[[Pinocchio (1940 film)|Pinocchio]]'' was the first animated feature film to win competitive Oscars, for [[Academy Award for Best Original Score|Best Original Score]] and [[Academy Award for Best Original Song|Best Original Song]], starting a long tradition of animated films winning in these categories. ''[[The Thief of Bagdad (1940 film)|The Thief of Bagdad]]'' received the most Oscars of the evening (3), the first time a film not nominated for Best Picture won the most awards. This and ''Pinocchio'' were the first films not nominated for Best Picture to receive multiple awards in Oscar history.

=== Special awards ===

* To [[Bob Hope]], in recognition of his unselfish services to the Motion Picture Industry.
* To Colonel [[Nathan Levinson]] for his outstanding service to the industry and the Army during the past nine years, which has made possible the present efficient mobilization of the motion picture industry facilities for the production of Army Training Films.

== Ceremony information ==
For the first time, names of all winners remained secret until the moment they received their awards, a practice that has continued ever since. [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] gave a six-minute direct radio address to the attendees from the [[White House]]. It is the first time an American president participated in the event.
